notes.title: Percentages and growth, computed
notes.body: A 12% raise on $85,000: 85,000 × 1.12 = **$95,200**. Compound growth: $100,000 at 7% for 5 years = 100,000 × 1.07⁵ = **$140,255** (not 100,000 × 1.35 — compounding beats simple multiplication). Rule of 72: at 7%, money doubles in ~72/7 ≈ 10.3 years. Always distinguish percentage points from percent: a raise from 5% to 7% bonus is +2 points but +40% relative.

notes.title: Expected value for decisions
Total compensation comparison
Mean vs median in salary data
Break-even analysis
Innumeracy traps
notes.body: Trap 1 — survivorship: 'our grads earn $150k' ignores dropouts. Trap 2 — small samples: 3 data points prove nothing. Trap 3 — relative vs absolute: '50% more interviews' from 2 to 3 is noise. Trap 4 — ignoring base rates (see the stats module's detector example). Defense: always ask 'compared to what, over what n, and who is missing?' Career decisions are quantitative: offers, growth, break-evens, and honest salary statistics.

notes.body: Everything in this module is practice material I authored for this course — the arc, the funnels, the story formats, the scenarios. Interstitium Labs confers no certificate, and nothing here is a credential, a job guarantee, or career advice about any specific employer. notes.title: Worked example: Customer asks for a dashboard. FDE first move?
Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Careers compound on evidence and relationships. In The Forward-Deployed Career, avoid:
- **One generic resume for every role.** Tailor or lose. Mirror the posting's language, lead with the employer's problem, and cut everything that doesn't serve this application.
- **Claims without artifacts.** 'Built X' with nothing to show is noise. Every major claim in The Forward-Deployed Career links to code, a writeup, a demo, or a reference.
- **Networking only when desperate.** Relationships built under pressure read as transactions. Build the network before you need it, with generosity first.
- **Skipping the debrief.** Every interview — win or lose — gets a written debrief within 24 hours: what they asked, how you answered, what you'd change.
- **Salary talk without research.** Never name a number you can't defend with market data. Research first, anchor deliberately, and get the full compensation picture.
- **Invisible work.** Doing good work that nobody can find. Ship publicly, write about it, and keep the portfolio current — discoverability is a career skill.

modules.summary: Welcome to IL-10, Portfolio, Career & Professional Practice — the career academy of the Interstitium Labs university. I'm your instructor for this course, and my job here is different from the technical tracks: the proof of work is already in your portfolio — this course turns it into a career you run deliberately. This is Module 1: The Forward-Deployed Career. Over this module we're going to run the six-move FDE arc — discover, model, prove, integrate, operate, generalize — and build the outcome layer on top of it: AI-matched applications tracked against skills you've actually earned, a conversion funnel that diagnoses its own bottlenecks, and interview systems for technical depth, system design, behavioral stories, and offers. By the end you'll have a career operating system, not a stack of good intentions.

notes.title: Concepts
Hands-on procedure
Project brief
notes.body:
**Project: the self-knowledge dossier.** Deliver a four-part brief you can actually use:
- **(1) Your result**, with borderline dichotomies flagged and interpreted as flexible — no fixed labels.
- **(2) A one-page working-style profile** — 'I do my best deep work when...' — written in language you can use verbatim in interviews.
- **(3) A team-composition plan** for a hypothetical four-person project: the four styles, what each contributes, and the failure mode if the finisher (or the diplomat) is missing.
- **(4) A one-quarter development plan**: one non-preferred function, one observable stretch behavior, and the review date.
This dossier is a career artifact: it feeds your interview answers, your team choices, and your quarterly reviews.

modules.summary: Welcome back — I'm your instructor, and this is Module 2: Self-Knowledge. You can't direct a career you haven't examined, so before we build ventures or climb ladders, we're going to take the Jung-typology instrument — the Humanmetrics assessment — and treat it as exactly what it is: working-style data for career decisions. Not a box, not a destiny, not a hiring tool — data. You'll learn what the four dichotomies actually measure, how to map type to role-family fit as a hypothesis, how to compose teams from complementary styles, and how to write a development plan that grows your range instead of replacing who you are.

**Project: the quant-ladder plan.** Deliver a written plan with five parts:
- **(1) A prerequisite audit** with honest gap flags: calculus, linear algebra, and probability at proof level (not cookbook); Python and C++. Gaps get study blocks, not wishful thinking.
- **(2) A 12-week probability-depth schedule**: timed problem sets, coins-and-dice at depth, code interviews where you implement the math (stochastic simulation in an hour).
- **(3) An internship timeline** worked backward from your target summers — applications and interviews a year ahead.
- **(4) A MicroMasters preparation map**: which IL-02/IL-10 nodes prepare each graduate course, plus a transfer-math worksheet — credit terms verified with MIT before enrolling.

notes.title: Honesty note
Worked example: Biggest predictor of quant interview success?
Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Careers compound on evidence and relationships. In Quantitative Finance: The Ladder, avoid:
- **One generic resume for every role.** Tailor or lose. Mirror the posting's language, lead with the employer's problem, and cut everything that doesn't serve this application.
- **Claims without artifacts.** 'Built X' with nothing to show is noise. Every major claim in Quantitative Finance: The Ladder links to code, a writeup, a demo, or a reference.
- **Networking only when desperate.** Relationships built under pressure read as transactions. Build the network before you need it, with generosity first.
- **Skipping the debrief.** Every interview — win or lose — gets a written debrief within 24 hours: what they asked, how you answered, what you'd change.
- **Salary talk without research.** Never name a number you can't defend with market data. Research first, anchor deliberately, and get the full compensation picture.
- **Invisible work.** Doing good work that nobody can find. Ship publicly, write about it, and keep the portfolio current — discoverability is a career skill.

scriptLabs.title: The Application Funnel Tracker
scriptLabs.brief: Build the funnel tracker: applications in, conversion at each stage, bottleneck diagnosis. The feedback loop as code.
scriptLabs.starter:
stages = ['applied','response','screen','onsite','offer']
counts = {'applied': 40, 'response': 12, 'screen': 8, 'onsite': 3, 'offer': 1}
# TODO: print conversion rate between consecutive stages
# TODO: print overall applied->offer rate
# TODO: diagnose the bottleneck (lowest conversion stage)
scriptLabs.solution:
stages = ['applied','response','screen','onsite','offer']
counts = {'applied': 40, 'response': 12, 'screen': 8, 'onsite': 3, 'offer': 1}
convs = {}
for i in range(len(stages)-1):
    r = counts[stages[i+1]]/counts[stages[i]]
    convs[f'{stages[i]}->{stages[i+1]}'] = r
    print(f'{stages[i]} -> {stages[i+1]}: {r:.1%}')
print(f'overall: {counts["offer"]/counts["applied"]:.1%}')
bottleneck = min(convs, key=convs.get)
print(f'bottleneck: {bottleneck} ({convs[bottleneck]:.1%})')
print('low response->resume/portfolio; low conversion->interviews; low offers->the close')
# Lesson: the funnel diagnoses itself — fix the bottleneck stage, not everything.

scriptLabs.title: Unit Economics Calculator
scriptLabs.brief: Model a venture's unit economics: CAC, LTV, payback, contribution margin. Verdict: scale, fix, or kill.
scriptLabs.starter:
cac = 120          # customer acquisition cost
arpu_mo = 25       # monthly revenue per user
margin = 0.8       # gross margin
churn_mo = 0.05    # monthly churn
# TODO: LTV, LTV:CAC, payback months, verdict
scriptLabs.hint: LTV = arpu*margin/churn. payback = cac/(arpu*margin). Bar: ratio>=3, payback<12.
scriptLabs.solution:
cac = 120
arpu_mo = 25
margin = 0.8
churn_mo = 0.05
ltv = arpu_mo*margin/churn_mo
ratio = ltv/cac
payback = cac/(arpu_mo*margin)
print(f'LTV=${ltv:.0f}  LTV:CAC={ratio:.1f}  payback={payback:.1f} mo')
if ratio >= 3 and payback < 12:
    print('verdict: SCALE — economics work')
elif ratio >= 2:
    print('verdict: FIX — improve retention or monetization before scale')
else:
    print('verdict: KILL or rebuild — scaling multiplies the loss')
# Lesson: unit economics before scale — the spreadsheet is the strategy.

scriptLabs.title: The Offer Evaluator
scriptLabs.brief: Score competing offers on total comp, growth, team, and your walk-away number. Decide like an adult, not from desperation.
scriptLabs.starter:
offers = [
    {'name':'A','base':95000,'bonus':10000,'equity_yr':15000,'growth':7,'team':8},
    {'name':'B','base':110000,'bonus':5000,'equity_yr':0,'growth':5,'team':6},
]
walk_away_total = 110000
# TODO: total comp per offer; score = total/walk_away weighted with growth, team
# TODO: print ranked recommendation
scriptLabs.solution:
offers = [
    {'name':'A','base':95000,'bonus':10000,'equity_yr':15000,'growth':7,'team':8},
    {'name':'B','base':110000,'bonus':5000,'equity_yr':0,'growth':5,'team':6},
]
walk_away_total = 110000
ranked = []
for o in offers:
    total = o['base']+o['bonus']+o['equity_yr']
    score = 0.6*(total/walk_away_total) + 0.2*(o['growth']/10) + 0.2*(o['team']/10)
    ranked.append((score, o['name'], total))
    print(f"{o['name']}: total=${total:,} score={score:.2f} {'BELOW WALK-AWAY' if total < walk_away_total else ''}")
for score, name, total in sorted(ranked, reverse=True):
    print(f'rank: {name} ({score:.2f})')
# Lesson: the walk-away number, decided in advance, prevents the worst mistake.

cheatSheets.title: The FDE career arc — discover to generalize

blocks.body: Find problems worth solving: talk to operators, read incident reports, follow the pain. A portfolio of solved real problems beats certificates.
Frame the problem precisely: inputs, outputs, constraints, success metric. If you can't state the metric, you don't understand the problem yet.
Build the smallest thing that proves the model: prototype, measurement, demo. Evidence over claims.
Ship into the real workflow: docs, handoff, monitoring. Unintegrated work is a hobby.
Run it, learn from production, then extract the pattern for the next problem. Careers compound on generalized patterns.
Narrate your reasoning aloud. Interviewers score the *process*: clarifying questions, tradeoff discussion, verification. Silent brilliance scores zero.
Requirements → capacity math → API → data model → components → scale/bottlenecks → failure modes. Always do the arithmetic.
Situation, Task, Action, Result — with numbers. Prepare 6–8 stories covering conflict, failure, leadership, ambiguity, and impact.
Total comp, growth slope, manager quality, team health, on-call load. The best offer is the best 2-year trajectory, not the biggest number.
Fall in love with the problem, not the solution. 20 customer conversations before code.
Minimum *viable*: the smallest test of the riskiest assumption. A landing page can be an MVP.
CAC vs LTV, gross margin, payback period. If the unit economics don't work, scale makes it worse.
SAFE notes, dilution, valuation caps, runway. Know what you're signing before you sign it.
Calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, programming (Python/C++) — honest self-rating per topic before anything else.
MIT's MicroMasters in Statistics and Data Science (or Finance): the structured bridge from audit to credibility.
Kaggle, research replication, trading simulations with honest backtests. Sharpe ratios without transaction costs are fiction.
The terminal rungs need research output or elite credentials. The ladder is honest about the cost of each step.

answerBank.a: FDE is a deployment model: you ship inside customer constraints and transfer operations. It suits people who like diagnosis, customers, and ambiguity. Pure SWE suits deep-system builders. The arc's skills transfer both ways.
Three excellent beats ten mediocre. Each with a README (problem, approach, results, proof link). Quality is the filter hiring managers actually apply.
It's a preference instrument, not a medical device — useful for working-style insight, not destiny. Use it for energy economics and team design; never for hiring decisions about others.
Default: job first, venture as the side project until unit economics or traction demand full time. Default alive applies to your life too — runway matters personally.
Desk quant roles hire at bachelor's/master's with proof-level math and C++/Python. Researcher roles skew PhD. The fork is real — audit honestly, then choose.

If you want the credential and the degree pathway: yes, with the transfer math done first. If you want only the knowledge: the preparation map (this module) plus the underlying math gets you most of the way.

terminalSims.title: Portfolio Project CLI
terminalSims.brief: Practice packaging proof-of-work: scaffold project entries, verify the four-link rule, and audit your portfolio for missing case studies.

commands.out:
Scaffolded: projects/ case-study/ demos/ README.md
Every project gets: problem, approach, outcome, links.

Added: zero-trust-lab
Next: write the case study — problem, approach, outcome, links.

Four-link rule: portfolio site [ok] GitHub [ok] LinkedIn [ok] demo URL [MISSING]
Fix the missing link before you ship.

Portfolio audit: 6 projects, 4 with case studies, 2 missing outcomes.
Ship the missing outcomes first — proof of work beats promises.

Template: 1) Problem 2) Constraints 3) Approach 4) Outcome (measured) 5) What you would do differently
Measured outcomes only — no adjectives without numbers.

terminalSims.title: Career Funnel CLI
terminalSims.brief: Track the job hunt like a pipeline: applications in, follow-ups out, walk-away numbers set before any negotiation.

commands.out:
Added to funnel: stage=applied
Follow-up scheduled in 7 days. Log the discovery notes now.

applied: 12 | screening: 3 | interview: 1 | offer: 0
Conversion applied→screening: 25%. Diagnose the funnel, not your worth.

Follow-up drafted: reference the discovery notes, one specific value-add, ask for the next step.
Never 'just checking in' — always add value.

Walk-away number: set BEFORE negotiation begins.
Integrate, don't capitulate — know your number before they name theirs.

Discovery template: role reality? hiring manager pain? success metric? timeline? budget?
The interview is mutual due diligence — you are evaluating them too.

glossary.definition: Forward-Deployed Engineer: embedded with customers, shipping solutions at the problem site — the course's career model.
Situation, Task, Action, Result: the structure for behavioral interview answers, with quantified results.
Minimum Viable Product: the smallest experiment testing the riskiest assumption.
Customer Acquisition Cost vs. Lifetime Value: the unit-economics pair every venture must get right.
Months until cash runs out at current burn; the startup's real deadline.
Simple Agreement for Future Equity: Y Combinator's standard early fundraising instrument.
MIT's graduate-level online credential series (e.g., Statistics and Data Science) — the quant ladder's bridge rung.
Simulating a trading strategy on historical data; honest backtests include transaction costs and slippage.
Risk-adjusted return: excess return per unit of volatility. High Sharpe on a backtest demands skepticism.
Comparing offers on total comp, growth slope, manager, team health, and on-call — not base salary alone.
Typology results used as self-knowledge for role fit — descriptive, not prescriptive.
The FDE arc's final step: extracting reusable patterns from operated solutions — how careers compound.

faq.q: What is the FDE career arc?
faq.a: Forward-Deployed Engineering as a career method: discover real problems, model them, prove solutions, integrate into workflows, operate, then generalize the patterns. It's the course's alternative to credential-collecting.

faq.q: How many STAR stories do I need?
faq.a: Six to eight, covering: conflict, failure, leadership without authority, ambiguity, technical depth, and measurable impact. Each with numbers. Rehearse aloud — written stories don't transfer to speech.
It's typology, not psychometrics — useful as structured self-reflection about working style, not as a validated predictor. The course uses it that way: data for decisions, not labels.

faq.q: Should I do a startup or get a job?
faq.a: The course is neutral but honest: ventures need 18+ months of runway thinking and a real problem; jobs compound skills and savings. Many do the job first, venture second — with the FDE arc either way.

faq.q: What's the quant ladder actually cost?
faq.a: 2–4 years of math/programming depth plus credential proof (MicroMasters → interviews). The module audits prerequisites honestly so you can price the climb before starting.

faq.q: How is this different from IL-13/14/15 interview prep?
faq.a: Those are *domain* interview prep (SWE, SRE/DevOps, data). IL-10 is the *career* layer: arc, narrative, ventures, and the quant path. Take IL-10 for strategy, the others for tactics.

faq.q: What makes a portfolio project hireable?
faq.a: A real problem, a clear metric, evidence it works (demo, measurements), and a write-up showing your reasoning. Three such projects beat thirty tutorial clones.

tips: Follow the guided path in order — each module unlocks the next. The sequence is the curriculum; skipping ahead breaks the chain.
Quiz-gated modules need 70%+ to unlock the next. When you miss a question, ask Noah to walk you through the miss Socratically before re-attempting.
Do each hands-on lab twice — once following the guide, once from a blank screen. The second pass is where the skill sticks.
This is a 29-hour course: about 8 hours a week finishes it in a month. Short daily sessions beat weekend cramming.
Mark a module complete only when you can teach it back in 90 seconds — explanation is the course's own bar for 'done'.
When spaced-review prompts surface, do them — they are pulled from your own earlier misses, which is exactly what needs repeating.
